title: What's Under the Paint Is Also by Him
standfirst: Frank Auerbach painted the same face, Estella West's, on and off for twenty-three years, and his method was to scrape back most of what he'd done the day before and start again. This head is what survived being started over the most times — not a beginning, but a last state sitting on top of everything he destroyed to get there.

sections.heading: A Method Built Out of Destroying the Day Before
sections.body:
Auerbach worked from the same small, damp Camden Town studio, bought around 1954, for the rest of his life. His way of making a picture was to paint it thickly and fast, leave the canvas to dry in a wooden box for days or weeks, then scrape the surface back and paint it again — sometimes for [as many as seventy sittings](https://art-now-and-then.blogspot.com/2016/08/frank-auerbach.html) before he judged one right. Almost none of the earlier attempts survive as image. What's left of them is structural: ridges and buried colour under the final layer, the physical residue of a picture that got painted, by his own hand, several dozen times before this version was allowed to stand.

He described the discipline behind it plainly enough: 'If you pass something every day and it has a little character, it begins to intrigue you.' Repetition wasn't a habit around the edges of his work. It was the work.

sections.heading: A Widow Twice His Age Who Became the Only Subject That Mattered
sections.body:
Auerbach met Estella Olive West in the late 1940s, cast opposite her in an amateur production of Peter Ustinov's House of Regrets. She was thirty-two, a widow who ran a boarding house; he was seventeen. He moved into the house not long after, and West became both his lover and, for something close to twenty-three years, his principal model — the sitter behind most of his female heads and nudes until the relationship ended abruptly in 1973.

He dated his own breakthrough as a painter to a session with her in the summer of 1952, when he found, as he put it, [the courage to repaint the whole thing](https://www.irishtimes.com/culture/art-and-design/a-second-family-for-frank-auerbach-1.2558704) 'from top to bottom, irrationally and instinctively' rather than patch at what wasn't working. The demolish-and-rebuild method that produced this head effectively starts there, in a room with her, years before it hardened into a daily rule.

sections.heading: A Red Cross Sewn Into a Coat, Then Silence
sections.body:
Auerbach was born in Berlin in April 1931 to Max Auerbach, a lawyer, and Charlotte Nora Borchardt, a former art student. In April 1939, not yet eight, he was put on a Kindertransport train to England, one of six children sponsored by the writers Iris and Antonio Origo. He never saw his parents again. His mother, sensing what was coming, sewed red crosses into the clothes she packed for him.

What happened to them afterwards is where the record stops agreeing with itself: most accounts say they were deported to Auschwitz and killed in 1942, one places their deaths a year later, and one obituary states he never established which camp they died in at all. Auerbach's own line on it, given late in life, was equanimity bordering on refusal: 'I think I did this thing which psychiatrists frown on: I am in total denial. It's worked very well for me.' He added, of the parents he lost at eight, 'there's just never been a point in my life when I felt I wished I had parents.'

sections.heading: Born Where Expressionism Was Invented, Filed Under It by Accident
sections.body:
This feature's own catalogue calls the movement here Expressionism, and it is easy to see why: the paint is thick enough in places to leave the canvas unable to hang flat. But Auerbach didn't train in the Germany that gave the word its first meaning — he trained in London, in David Bomberg's evening classes at Borough Polytechnic alongside Leon Kossoff, a generation and a continent removed from Kirchner or Nolde. Critics reaching for 'Expressionist' are describing what the paint does, not tracing a lineage back to the movement his own birth city produced and that he fled at seven.

The label historians actually settled on decades later was School of London, grouping Auerbach with Francis Bacon and Lucian Freud more for shared stubbornness about the human figure than for any common technique. David Sylvester, reviewing Auerbach's 1956 debut, called it the most exciting first show by an English painter [since Bacon's in 1949](https://www.tate.org.uk/art/artists/frank-auerbach-676) — and insisted, against the more obvious reading of all that crusted paint, that the results were 'painterly images, not sculptural ones.'

sections.heading: What the Last State Agrees to Keep
sections.body: No biographer draws a straight line from the canvases destroyed under this head to the disputed, half-recovered record of how Auerbach's parents actually died, and claiming one outright would be tidier than the evidence allows. But the practice is on the record regardless: a man without an agreed account of where or even when his parents were killed spent seventy years painting the same handful of faces specifically in order to erase most of what he tried and keep only the version that felt true on the day he stopped. The Sunday Times called him Britain's greatest living artist. He worked in the same Camden Town studio until his death in November 2024, aged ninety-three, having spent longer disagreeing with his own paintings than most painters spend making theirs.
